Abiy made the announcement on X on Wednesday during a visit to Moscow for the two-day Russia-Africa Summit, where Russia is seeking closer security and economic ties with African countries. The acquisition comes as Ethiopian forces fight renewed battles with rebels in northern Tigray and a separate rebellion in the neighbouring Amhara region. advertisements The prime minister said the warplanes had arrived a year earlier than expected under an existing agreement with Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin for helping speed up the delivery. He gave no date for the arrival of the S-400 batteries, designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles. Abiy said on Wednesday that the new equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”. In a second X post later that day, he described the jets as newly deployed and said they would defend Ethiopian airspace. Military cooperation The announcement is the latest sign of Russia‘s growing military partnership with Ethiopia, following a series of agreements in recent years. The two governments signed a military cooperation agreement in Addis Ababa in July 2021 aimed at improving the Ethiopian armed forces’ training and technology. In January, defence publication Janes reported that Ethiopia had displayed newly acquired Russian Yak-130 advanced jet trainers during celebrations marking its air force’s 90th anniversary. Russia supplied 15 percent of Africa’s imports of major weapons between 2021 and 2025, making it the continent’s third-largest supplier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Moscow has sought closer military and economic ties with African countries while facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. The Russia-Africa Summit, which began on Wednesday, brings African leaders together for talks on trade, investment and security. Tigray war The announcement follows a major shift in the fighting in Tigray, where government troops and allied forces entered the regional capital Mekelle on October 4 after fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew. The TPLF, an armed group that previously governed the region, has suffered further territorial losses as government forces advanced into other towns. Addis Ababa has since appointed a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, but the fighting has not stopped. A TPLF commander called for continued resistance in a television broadcast last week, while the group has also claimed attacks against government-aligned troops in northwestern Tigray on Wednesday. The renewed war has effectively undone a peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 that ended two years of fighting, which researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimate killed about 500,000 civilians. Government forces are also battling Fano, an Amhara armed group that has been fighting federal troops since 2023. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Russian Su-35 Deal Raises Questions Over Egypt's National Security Follow us Sada Elbalad Group Egypt Middle East World Business Tourism Culture & heritage Lifestyle More entertainment Sports Science & Tech opinion In depth Videos & Features Photo Gallery Supervisor Elham AbolFateh Editor-in-chief Safaa Nawar Home / Egypt EGYPT 2 min read Add as Preferred Source Ethiopia's Russian Su-35 Deal Raises Questions Over Egypt's National Security H-Tayea Egypt · Thu 29 Oct 2026 | 11:30 PM Ethiopia's Russian Su-35 Deal The director of the Russia Federal News Network (RFN) has sought to reassure Egyptians over Russia's military cooperation with Ethiopia, arguing that Addis Ababa's acquisition of advanced Russian fighter jets and planned air defence systems should not automatically be interpreted as a threat to Egyptian national security. The remarks followed Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's announcement on 28 October that his country had acquired 12 Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and would receive four batteries of the S-400 air defence system. The announcement raised questions about regional military capabilities, particularly against the background of longstanding disagreements between Egypt and Ethiopia over Nile water security and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). Russian Media Official Addresses Egyptian Security Concerns In a statement addressing the controversy, the RFN director said Ethiopia's acquisition of advanced Russian weapons did not establish that Egypt was the intended target of the military cooperation. He argued that possessing sophisticated fighter aircraft was different from having the operational capability to conduct successful long-range military operations. Such operations depend on several factors, including pilot training, logistical support, maintenance, operational readiness and the integration of aircraft with other military systems. The official also noted that the S-400 is primarily an air defence system designed to intercept aerial threats rather than conduct offensive strikes. He urged Egyptians to distinguish between legitimate national security concerns and conclusions unsupported by confirmed evidence. Egypt's Previous Su-35 Deal And US Sanctions The statement also addressed Egypt's earlier efforts to acquire Russian Su-35 fighters. Reports in 2018 and 2019 indicated that Cairo had arranged to purchase more than 20 aircraft in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion. However, the acquisition encountered significant obstacles after Washington warned that purchasing advanced Russian military equipment could expose Egypt to sanctions under the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA). The reported deal subsequently stalled, and Egypt did not publicly confirm taking delivery of the aircraft. The RFN director maintained that Russia's military cooperation with Ethiopia should not be interpreted as a shift against Egypt, given the longstanding strategic relationship between Cairo and Moscow. Russia-Egypt Relations Remain Central To Regional Cooperation The remarks followed talks between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on 28 October, during which they discussed regional security, bilateral cooperation and developments in the Horn of Africa. El-Sisi reiterated that Nile water security was an existential issue for Egypt and rejected unilateral measures affecting the Eastern Nile Basin. The RFN director stressed the importance of safeguarding Egypt's stability while avoiding exaggerated assessments of regional military developments. He described Egyptian national security as closely connected to Russian national security, concluding that the two countries were pursuing a common path. #Ethiopia # Russia # Egypt # Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets H-Tayea Contributor at SEE News — Sada Elbalad English. The research, published in Discover Food, evaluated the program’s impact on rural households using survey data collected from 124 households, split evenly between 62 program beneficiaries and 62 non-beneficiaries. The researchers analyzed the data with both descriptive statistics and econometric methods. A Difference-in-Differences estimation indicated that the program had a positive and statistically significant impact on the food security of beneficiary households. The same analysis found that family size had a negative effect on household food security, suggesting that larger households in the study area faced greater difficulty maintaining adequate food access. In addition to the Difference-in-Differences approach, the study employed a binary logit model to estimate the factors associated with improvement in household food security. According to the results, beneficiary households had a significantly higher probability of improving their food security than non-beneficiary households, reinforcing the finding that program participation was linked to better food security outcomes in the study population. The study is limited to households in a single woreda and relies on a survey sample of 124 households, so the findings describe this specific study area rather than the program’s effects across Ethiopia as a whole. The authors recommend that the Productive Safety Net Program continue to be implemented, with adjustments to strengthen its contribution to household asset accumulation alongside its food security gains. Técnicas Reunidas announced on Wednesday that it would design, procure materials for, manufacture and deliver the two units within 18 months. The reformers are expected to produce a combined output of more than 200,000 normal cubic metres of hydrogen per hour. The company did not disclose the contract's value. The equipment will be supplied through TR-Technical, the Spanish company's heat-transfer equipment division, using process technology licensed by Danish firm Topsoe. The Gode complex is designed to produce three million tonnes of urea annually. Dangote and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed launched construction in October 2025, following a shareholders' agreement between Dangote Group and Ethiopian Investment Holdings, the state-owned investment fund. Dangote Group holds a 60% stake in the venture, while the Ethiopian entity owns the remaining 40%. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Initially valued at $2.5 billion, the project's investment estimate increased to more than $4 billion in May as plans expanded to include a 110-kilometre gas pipeline, a 120-megawatt power plant, a packaging facility and a blending plant with an annual capacity of two million tonnes of NPK fertiliser, Billionaires.Africa reported. The plant will use natural gas from the Calub field in the Ogaden basin. Chinese firm GCL Group signed a 25-year supply agreement in March, according to the report. Ethiopia currently imports nearly all its fertiliser, and the government expects domestic production to reduce foreign currency expenditure and support agricultural output. Earlier this month, Dangote said he planned to offer at least 10% of the Ethiopian venture to local investors through the Ethiopian Securities Exchange once production stabilises. No date or pricing has been announced for the proposed share sale. Addis Standard reported in August 2025 that Ethiopian Investment Holdings (EIH), the government's strategic investment arm, and Dangote Group had signed a shareholders' agreement to develop a $2.5 billion urea fertiliser complex in Gode, Somali Region. Under the agreement, Dangote Group holds a 60% stake in the joint venture, while EIH owns the remaining 40%. In May 2026, Addis Standard reported that the planned investment had increased to more than $4 billion following a visit to the construction site by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote. The expanded project includes a gas pipeline from the Calub field in the Ogaden Basin, a 120-megawatt power plant, a polypropylene packaging facility and a blending plant designed to produce two million tonnes of NPK fertiliser annually. Following the visit, Abiy described the initiative as a strategic investment in Ethiopia's agricultural transformation, food security and economic self-reliance. He said the facility would strengthen domestic production, reduce import dependence, support farmers and create employment opportunities. The government has also sought to accelerate construction beyond the original 40-month timeline. In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on a $4.2 billion, 25-year natural gas supply agreement between Dangote Industries Limited and China's GCL Group. The agreement provides for gas from the Calub field to supply the complex, linking domestic gas extraction with fertiliser production. Turkey is one of Somalia’s key military partners, providing training, equipment and technical assistance to Somali security forces. Ankara operates a major military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali soldiers as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities. The two countries have also expanded their military relationship through defence and maritime security agreements aimed at improving Somalia’s capacity to protect its territorial waters and combat security threats. The planned deployment of the two warships comes as Somalia and Turkey continue to deepen their military partnership, including cooperation on training, maritime security and defence capacity-building. Uganda was first to send forces into Somalia under Amisom, and has maintained the largest contingent in the country. PHOTO/ATMIS By Job Bwire Websites Editor NMG-U What you need to know: Continental leadership has maintained that support for Somalia's peace transition will endure. During the July summit, the Chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mr Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, reassured the region of continued backing while paying tribute to the peacekeeping troops. Uganda has officially commenced the withdrawal of the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) from Somalia after nearly two decades of active involvement, marks a major milestone in the country's military engagement in the Horn of Africa. The Chief of Defence Forces (CDF), Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, confirmed the development on Thursday, signaling the start of a security handover to the host nation. "As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," Gen Muhoozi posted on X on October 29, 2026. The withdrawal comes amid mounting financial constraints and major diplomatic shifts surrounding the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). In July 2026, the United States informed the African Union that it would not support renewing the mission’s mandate before the United Nations Security Council in December, alongside a 25 percent funding cut by the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) that has impacted frontline operations. Related Muhoozi rallies African military chiefs as UN cuts threaten Somalia peace mission National Jul 30 Africa will stand by Somalia if donors pull out- Museveni National Aug 01 READ : Why Uganda keeps troops in Somalia UPDF’s long battle to save Somalia from destruction Lone wolf: UPDF soldiers on in Somalia, but at what cost? Despite these growing international funding cuts, Ugandan authorities had earlier indicated that regional solidarity would remain intact regardless of foreign financial support. Addressing the Extraordinary Summit of Heads of State of Troop-Contributing Countries at Speke Resort Munyonyo on July 31, 2026, President Museveni declared that African nations possess the resilience to tackle security challenges on their own. "If the international community wants to pull out, let them. All the problems we have solved here, we solved without their support. We got support from our brothers. When we fought Amin, it was Tanzania and Mozambique. On Sudan, it was us. Somalia will not be abandoned. We have the capacity. Whether others pull out or not, we shall stand," President Museveni stated. The President defended Uganda's initial 2007 deployment, explaining that the military intervention was driven by regional security imperatives and principle rather than foreign interests. "When therefore we decided to involve ourselves in Somalia, it was out of principle and strategy. We did not accept the chauvinism of Islamic groups who come here and waste our time... The second reason was to extend solidarity to Ethiopia... We had to stand with them," Mr Museveni noted. ALSO READ : UPDF Somalia casualties flown back today- Army During the pre-summit military deliberations in July, Gen Muhoozi called on regional defense leaders to adapt to shrinking international resources and establish self-sustaining African-led operational frameworks before UNSOS wraps up its logistical support by December 31, 2026. "These are difficult circumstances, but they also call for our unity, creativity, and resolve," Gen Muhoozi told regional military chiefs. "The future of our mission, and the sacrifice and progress we have all made together in Somalia, depend on the quality of the decisions we make at moments like this. As Chiefs of Defence Forces, we are responsible for providing clear military guidance and strategic direction at a time when the mission environment is changing." Continental leadership has maintained that support for Somalia's peace transition will endure. During the July summit, the Chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mr Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, reassured the region of continued backing while paying tribute to the peacekeeping troops. "I wish to assure the government and people of Somalia that the Commission will continue to mobilize all the political, diplomatic, and financial support necessary for the success of this mission," Mr Youssouf said. Somalia’s military leadership also recognized the role played by foreign troops in stabilizing the nation over the past two decades. Expressing gratitude to the troop-contributing nations, the Commander of the Somali National Armed Forces, Brig Gen Ibrahim Mohamed Mahmoud, commended the peacekeeping forces for their long-standing sacrifices. Echoing this sentiment, the Head of the AU Peace Support Operations Division, Brig Gen Cheick Dembele, emphasized that unbroken African solidarity remains vital as the continent works toward building robust Somali security institutions capable of maintaining lasting peace. Uganda made history in 2007 as the first nation to deploy troops to Somalia under the original African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM). Over the last 19 years, the UPDF played a central role alongside the Somali National Army in liberating key strategic territories from the Al-Shabaab militant group and safeguarding critical government infrastructure. Following AMISOM's transition into AUSSOM in 2024, the mission shifted focus toward strengthening Somali national security bodies, protecting civilians, and preparing Somali forces for a full takeover of national security. somalia.content: Somalia’s political future is at risk - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia’s political future is at risk Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Dr. Ali Said Faqi Thursday October 29, 2026 Somalia’s Third Republic was established as a federal country because no durable national government could be rebuilt through domination by the center. Federalism was intended to distribute power, accommodate regional interests and hold together a country fractured by decades of conflict. Today, that political settlement is under serious strain. Disputes over the Constitution, the electoral model and the division of authority have pushed the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), several Federal Member States (FMS) and opposition groups toward confrontation. In Southwest State, that confrontation has become military. In this piece, I examine how disputes over federalism, constitutional amendments, the president’s expired mandate and the electoral process have brought Somalia to this point. I argue that the crisis cannot be resolved through unilateral decisions or force; it requires an inclusive political settlement that restores trust and keeps the national army out of partisan conflict. advertisements Puntland and Jubaland have rejected the federal government’s constitutional process, while other political actors accuse Villa Somalia of weakening the autonomy of the FMS and concentrating power in Mogadishu. The FGS argues that direct elections and stronger national institutions are necessary to move Somalia beyond repeated elite bargaining. That objective has merit. But a democratic system cannot gain legitimacy when one side determines the rules and imposes them on the rest of the country. The FGS’s approach toward the member states has therefore been interpreted as an attempt to dismantle federalism rather than reform it. The president points to voting conducted in parts of Southwest State, Galmudug and Hirshabelle as evidence that Somalia is advancing toward one-person, one-vote elections. Yet these processes were widely regarded by Somalis as selections rather than genuine elections. Political competition was restricted, outcomes were heavily managed, and voters were not offered a meaningful choice. Despite this, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has presented them as victories for democratization. Democracy cannot be measured by the opening of polling stations alone; it requires genuine competition, institutional independence and public confidence in the result. The electoral timetable has intensified the dispute as well. The president’s electoral commission has announced parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, followed by a presidential election on May 15. Opposition groups reject the timetable because it was announced without agreement on the electoral framework, administration of the vote or constitutional basis for extending the current political arrangement. Much of the opposition supports direct elections in principle but disputes a process controlled by Villa Somalia. The unilateral timetable has also fueled rumors that the president intends to proceed with an election on his own terms, declare himself the winner and remain in office even if his authority is reduced to Villa Somalia. Whether or not this is his plan, the fact that such fears are circulating reflects the depth of mistrust and makes an agreed political process more urgent. That disagreement is also tied directly to the president’s mandate. Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s four-year term expired on May 15, 2026. In January 2024, he publicly assured Somalis that constitutional changes, particularly any change affecting the presidential term, would apply to the next legislative term, not the current one. Two months later, amendments were approved changing the terms of federal institutions from four to five years. The president now relies on those amendments to justify remaining in office until May 2027. His current position contradicts his earlier assurance. The opposition maintains that the amendments cannot be applied retroactively to extend a mandate obtained under the previous four-year arrangement. The president’s decision to proceed under the amended electoral model, including changes to how national leaders are elected, has deepened the constitutional crisis and damaged trust. The president is expected to uphold the Constitution and serve as a symbol of national unity, especially during a political crisis. His responsibility is to keep the country together while addressing competing national interests. When he becomes a party to the dispute rather than a credible mediator, the presidency loses its unifying role. The proposed consultative forum in Mogadishu from November 14 to 18 has not restored confidence. The invitation alone is insufficient, particularly after repeated failures to negotiate with opposition groups, even following international efforts to resolve the electoral disagreement. Many stakeholders suspect the invitation is intended to buy time rather than produce an agreement. That mistrust is reinforced by Villa Somalia’s failure to offer a clear agenda, agreed ground rules or a mutually accepted process for the dialogue. It has not explained how participants would shape the agenda or influence decisions already announced. Unless opposition concerns are addressed, the forum may not take place in any meaningful form. A meeting controlled entirely by the presidency would amount to political management, not negotiation. The political standoff is also playing out on the ground in Southwest State. In March, federal forces entered Baidoa, removed the administration of President Abdiaziz Laftagareen and supported a replacement authority. Armed confrontation has continued, with forces loyal to Laftagareen regaining several district centers and putting pressure on routes leading to Baidoa. The use of federal forces in this struggle has turned a political dispute into an internal armed conflict. That conflict is also diverting the Somali National Army from the national security role it is expected to assume as African Union forces draw down. The SNA is not ready to replace those forces across the country; some areas transferred to Somali forces have since returned to Al-Shabaab control. Using the army against domestic political opponents further weakens its ability to secure the country and undermines public confidence in its national mission. It also damages public confidence and creates opportunities for Al-Shabaab to expand. The continuing confrontation in Southwest State and the diversion of the SNA into internal political conflict make a negotiated settlement urgent. The immediate priority should be to de-escalate the fighting and keep the army out of partisan disputes. The president, FMS leaders and opposition groups should then enter negotiations under a process with a jointly agreed agenda and ground rules, with facilitation acceptable to all parties. Talks must address the disputed constitutional amendments, the president’s mandate and the electoral timetable, and produce a roadmap that all sides agree to respect. Without such an agreement, competing electoral processes, rival claims to legitimacy and further armed confrontation remain real risks. The central test is whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud will accept a negotiated electoral settlement that the federal member states and opposition can trust. Somalia’s political future depends on that choice. somalia.summary: Somalia's political future is increasingly precarious as tensions rise between the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), Federal Member States (FMS), and opposition groups. Established as a federal system to distribute power and accommodate regional interests, the political framework is now under severe strain due to disputes over the Constitution, electoral processes, and the president's expired mandate. The situation has escalated into military confrontations, particularly in Southwest State, where federal forces have intervened. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's unilateral electoral timetable and constitutional amendments have deepened mistrust, as opposition groups fear he may attempt to extend his term without consensus. The proposed consultative forum in November has failed to restore confidence, with many viewing it as a tactic to delay meaningful negotiations. The ongoing conflict not only threatens political stability but also diverts the Somali National Army from its security role, exacerbating vulnerabilities to groups like Al-Shabaab. A negotiated settlement addressing these issues is urgently needed to secure Somalia's future.

Briefs {{series.title}} Full List {{series.title}} {{series.description | limitTo:140}} {{series.fb_title}} × 8 hours ago Al Shabaab Ambush in South West State; Algeria Deploys to Niger: Africa File, October 29, 2026 Michael DeAngelo and Liam Karr To receive the Africa File, Ethiopia War Security Review, or Congo War Security Review via email, please subscribe here . Follow CTP on X , LinkedIn , and BlueSky . Contributors: Ziv Zellars and Tyler Davila Key Takeaways: Somalia . Al Shabaab ambushed Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) forces, who had launched a counteroffensive against opposition forces in South West state, inflicting mass casualties on federal forces. Tensions between the FGS and local factions in central and south-central Somalia have provided openings for al Shabaab to exploit, including by potentially coordinating with opposition forces. Algeria . Algeria authorized a troop deployment to northern Niger, likely to advance several shared economic and security objectives in Niger. The deployments are part of Algeria’s new, more assertive approach to its Sahel strategy, which aims to outcompete its North African neighbors, Morocco and the eastern Libyan Haftar regime. Figure 1. Africa File, October 29, 2026 Source: Emily Bjerke. Assessments: Somalia Author: Michael DeAngelo with Ziv Zellars Al Shabaab ambushed Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) forces, who had launched a counteroffensive against opposition forces in South West state, inflicting mass casualties on federal forces. South West state opposition forces captured five key towns in the Bay region from October 8 to 16, including Buurhakaba, which is 40 miles southeast of Baidoa, the de facto South West state capital. [1] The FGS subsequently announced that it would mount a counteroffensive, Operation Banooda, and the anti-FGS Somali news outlets Baidoa Online and Somali Guardian reported that the Somali military had deployed over 200 military vehicles and 2,000 soldiers toward Buurhakaba from the nearby Baledogle Airfield by October 26. [2] Al Shabaab halted the advance and inflicted mass casualties on federal forces when it ambushed the federal reinforcements on October 26 near the town of Leego, which is 30 miles southeast of Buurhakaba. Al Shabaab claimed to have killed 413 federal soldiers, wounded or captured more federal personnel, and captured and destroyed at least several Somali military vehicles, reportedly including Turkish armored vehicles. [3] Reuters and Baidoa Online cited federal security sources who said that several dozen soldiers had died, with one Reuters source reporting over 140 casualties. [4] Figure 2. Al Shabaab Ambushes Federal Forces in South West State Source: Michael DeAngelo; Liam Karr; Hannah Ochs; Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED). Vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and attack drones, the latter of which al Shabaab has not publicly confirmed to have used before, reportedly targeted federal forces during the ambush. The Somali Ministry of Defense confirmed that al Shabaab used vehicle-borne IEDs, which damaged several Somali military vehicles. [5] Multiple Somali outlets also reported that one-way attack drones and drones rigged to drop explosives targeted federal forces near Leego, although the Critical Threats Project (CTP) could not confirm the reports. [6] Unverified reports indicated that Turkish fighter jets or drones accidently struck Somali federal forces when providing them with air support, however, although the Somali Office of National Security denied the reports. [7] Al Shabaab has previously used drones for propaganda and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, rather than attacks. [8] The United Nations and Africa Center for Strategic Studies have reported that al Shabaab members have received advanced weapons training from the Yemeni Houthis and sought to acquire attack drones, however. [9] The FGS has sought to downplay the ambush, although the activity of Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud indicate that the attack has alarmed the FGS. The Somali Ministry of Defense released a statement on October 27 not acknowledging any losses and instead claiming that federal forces had killed nearly 75 al Shabaab militants and wounded another 56. [10] Mohamud’s cabinet reportedly held an emergency meeting on October 27, however, and the Somali Stream news outlet reported that Mohamud canceled his planned trip to the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow from October 28 to October 29. [11] The Somali defense ministry reaffirmed its intent to continue Operation Banooda and reported that the head of the Somali National Army’s ground forces visited “front-line positions” near Leego on October 28. [12] Baidoa Online reported on October 28 that the Somali military is deploying additional forces to the area. [13] Tensions between the FGS and local factions in central and south-central Somalia have provided openings for al Shabaab to exploit, including by potentially coordinating with opposition forces. The FGS deposed former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed (Laftagareen) in March 2026 to establish a pro-FGS state administration, causing an opposition uprising by Laftagareen-aligned forces since May that federal and state forces have been unable to quell. [14] CTP has recorded eight sets of clashes between opposition and state forces in or on the outskirts of Baidoa, among other locations, with the most recent occurring on October 26. [15] Al Shabaab has taken advantage of the instability by increasing its activity in South West and almost certainly deconflicting and possibly coordinating with opposition forces in the state. The Salafi-jihadi group has increased monthly attacks in South West by approximately 25 percent since the FGS deposed Laftagareen, compared with its previous monthly average in 2026. [16] Al Shabaab may also be coordinating with the South West opposition forces amid repeated FGS and South West state government accusations of al Shabaab participation in opposition attacks since August. [17] Vehicle-borne IEDs, which al Shabaab has relied on as a key tactic for years, have reportedly targeted federal and South West state forces during clashes with the opposition forces. [18] South West opposition forces have also moved freely through al Shabaab support zones to capture towns where al Shabaab has applied long-term pressure, including Buurhakaba. [19] South West opposition officials have repeatedly denied that opposition forces are collaborating with al Shabaab. [20] Figure 3. Al Shabaab Increases Activity Following Federal Takeover in South West State, 2026 Source: Michael DeAngelo; Ziv Zellars; ACLED. The FGS is separately embroiled in an escalating political dispute with the influential Hawadle clan in Hirshabelle state’s Hiiraan region. Hawadle members have challenged the recent Hirshabelle state election in which the FGS’s favored candidate, who is from a different clan in the Middle Shabelle region, won reelection, arguing that the state presidency should switch to the Hawadle clan according to traditional power-sharing agreements. [21] Hirshabelle State Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed, who is Hawadle and reportedly seeks the state presidency, stated that he will not vacate his seat until a settlement is reached. [22] Former Somali intelligence head Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbalolshe, who is also Hawadle, recently stated that the clan plans to form a new regional government in Hiiraan. [23] Sanbalolshe also claimed that he had met in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with the leaders of the Jubbaland and Puntland states and Somaliland, all of whom oppose the FGS, to seek support for an armed uprising against the FGS. [24] Several Somali news outlets reported on October 27 that Hawadle militiamen have begun mobilizing around Beledweyne, the Hiiraan regional capital. [25] Al Shabaab has made inroads with the Hawadle amid the political dispute in Hirshabelle despite long-standing animus between the group and the clan. Al Shabaab announced an agreement in early October to cease hostilities with influential Hawadle factions. [26] Hawadle militiamen previously played a key role in the federally backed counterterrorism offensive against al Shabaab in 2022 and 2023. [27] Sanbalolshe reportedly did not rule out collaborating with al Shabaab when discussing plans to oppose the FGS in late October. [28] Al Shabaab separately conducted its first operations against government forces in northern Somalia's Puntland state since early 2024. Al Shabaab has detonated two IEDs and conducted a mortar attack around Galgala—40 miles south of Bosaso, Puntland’s main port city—since October 19. [29] The attacks injured several people and killed a Puntland state soldier. [30] Al Shabaab had previously shifted its attention away from Puntland after the Islamic State Somalia Province (ISS) had gained the upper hand in their inter-jihadi rivalry by early 2024. [31] ISS’s preeminence resulted in a US- and Emirati-backed Puntland state counteroffensive that greatly weakened the group. [32] Puntland state partners have immediately responded to al Shabaab’s increased activity. The US Africa Command conducted an airstrike against al Shabaab militants in the Cal Madow mountains between Bosaso and Galgala on October 19. [33] The UAE also reportedly conducted two airstrikes against al Shabaab militants in the same area on October 20 and 21, the first reported Emirati strikes in Puntland since the FGS canceled bilateral agreements with the UAE in January 2026. [34] Open-source analyst Rich Tedd has reported an uptick in suspected Emirati activity at Bosaso airport since mid-September 2026, although it is unclear whether this is tied to Emirati activity in Somalia or elsewhere in the Horn of Africa. [35] Agence France-Presse also cited two Puntland state officials who stated that the Puntland state government plans to announce an offensive against al Shabaab in the near future. [36] Algeria Authors: Liam Karr and Victoria Hutchinson with Tyler Davila Algeria authorized a troop deployment to northern Niger as it implements its new, more assertive approach to its Sahel strategy. Algeria’s Parliament approved a resolution authorizing the deployment of army units to northern Niger on October 25, two days after Algeria’s Parliament summoned all members to an emergency meeting to discuss a possible military intervention in Niger. [37] Nigerien Minister of State and National Defense General Salifou Modi had met with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on October 21 before signing a new military and defense cooperation agreement with Algerian General of the Army Saïd Chengriha that same day. [38] This was Modi’s second working visit with General Chengriha in just over a week, following an October 13 meeting in Algiers where they discussed border security and counterterrorism efforts. [39] Algeria has hosted visits by Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tiani, Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine, and General Modi over the past month. [40] Algeria has had forces in Niger since it deployed air squadrons in support of the Nigerien junta during the attempted coup in Niamey in late August. Algeria sent four Russian-made Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jets, an Ilyushin Il-78 refueling aircraft, and an Ilyushin Il-76 military transport plane, and their support teams to Niamey after disgruntled Nigerien forces attempted to overthrow Nigerien junta leader Abdourahamane Tiani on August 29. [41] The fighter jets remain stationed at Diori Hamani International Airport and Air Base 101 in Niamey. [42] CTP previously assessed that Algeria’s response to the Niger coup attempt could signal that it is taking a more assertive approach to protecting its interests in the Sahel. The recent parliamentary approval would mark Algeria’s first foreign troop deployment since it sent troops to Egypt to fight against Israel in the 1973 War. [43] Algeria has historically exercised a noninterventionist foreign policy and did not legally support foreign deployments until constitutional amendments in 2020. [44] This decision comes amid rekindling relations between Algeria and its Sahelian neighbors, after a diplomatic rupture following Algeria’s downing of a Malian drone near their shared border in April 2025. Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew their ambassadors to Algeria after Algeria shot down a Malian drone over the border town of Tinzaouaten in April 2025. [45] President Tebboune hosted President Tiani from February 15 through 16 to mend diplomatic relations, and in early August Algeria donated two Mi-24V attack helicopters and two Mi-171 helicopters. [46] The improved relations between Algeria and Niger likely helped facilitate Algeria’s subsequent rapprochement with Mali. [47] Malian forces and their Russian allies took the regional capital Kidal town in northern Mali—which the Azawad Liberation Front ( Front de Libération de l’Azawad , FLA) and its al Qaeda–linked allies Jama'at Nusrat al Islam wa al Muslimeen had held since April—on October 6. [48] President Tebboune reaffirmed two days before the operation that Algeria would “step up” if Mali or Niger asked, and Algerian forces reportedly closed the border as operations were ongoing to prevent rebels from fleeing into Algeria. [49] The deployments likely aim to advance several shared economic and security objectives in Niger. The Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune stated that troops will be deployed to northern Niger to “protect energy and economic interests” in Niger. Algeria’s state-owned oil company Sonatrach has been collaborating with Niger and Nigeria on the $13 billion Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP) since 2009, but the project was largely dormant until the countries signed a series of agreements in 2022 to begin crucial preconstruction work. [50] The TSGP is planned to run roughly 2,565 miles from southern Nigeria through Niger to Algeria’s Hassi R’Mel gas hub, and the pipeline is expected to transport as much as 30 billion cubic meters of natural gas per year when completed. [51] The new section, slated for construction in early 2027, will stretch roughly 750 miles from Algeria’s border with Niger to Aoulef in southern Algeria before connecting with Algeria’s existing pipeline network. [52] Sonatrach has also recently advanced several agreements for several oil sites in Niger, including an oil refinery in the southern Zinder region and two oil drilling sites near the Algerian border in northern Niger’s Agadez region that Sonatrach claims hold a combined 268 million barrels of proven reserves. [53] Algeria inaugurated a four-well drilling site in Kafra, obtained an exploration permit for Bilma, and signed a partnership agreement to provide technical maintenance and training at the Zinder refinery—all in August 2026. GNS stands for Government of National Stability. MPLJ stands for Mouvement Patriotique pour la Liberté et la Justice (Patriotic Movement for Liberty and Justice). SLOR stands for Southern Liberation Operations Room. Source: Liam Karr; ACLED. The Algerian parliament resolution explicitly authorized the deployment of troops to Madama, a critical outpost for influencing trans-Saharan trafficking and rebel networks. [55] The base in the area is located in the Bilma department, approximately 60 miles south and 150 miles southeast of the Libyan and Algerian borders, which makes it vital for monitoring the movement of arms, drugs, fuel, goods, and people between southern Libya and the Sahel. [56] The Sahara border zone has long served as a rear base for numerous armed groups operating across the Sahel-Sahara region, as it is a largely ungoverned space with gold and oil deposits and trafficking networks between North Africa and sub-Saharan Africa. [57] Chadian, Libyan, and Nigerien rebel groups have relocated to the Agadez region in northern Niger in recent years due to heightened pressure on the Chadian and Libyan sides of the border and Niger’s lack of capacity to control its side of the border. [58] The Nigerien groups in the area have attacked oil pipelines in other areas of Niger and aim to overthrow Algeria’s partners in the Nigerien junta. [59] Algeria and Niger may also be seeking to contain the influence of the eastern Libya–based Haftar regime, which has sought to increase its influence in the Sahel-Sahara border zone to control rebel and trafficking networks linked to southern Libya and strengthen ties with international partners amid intensified efforts to reunify Libya. Haftar-aligned forces began to turn a blind eye to Nigerien rebel groups in the border area in 2025 in response to Niger’s failure to control its side of the border and reportedly began strengthening ties with Nigerien rebel groups in mid-2026 in retaliation for Niger’s growing ties with the rival western Libya–based Government of National Unity (GNU). [60] The Haftar regime and Chad operationalized a joint border force in February 2026 and have launched operations led by the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF, also known as the Libyan National Army) into Chadian and Nigerien territory to target Chadian and Libyan rebels throughout 2026, but these efforts have seemingly not targeted the Nigerien rebel groups, including the Patriotic Liberation Front ( Front Patriotique de Libération, FPL), which have rear bases in Chad and Libya. [61] The LAAF has also cracked down on all fuel trade with Niger to prevent fuel from reaching rebel groups based in the northern Niger border area, indirectly affecting Nigerien border communities and patronage networks. [62] The Haftar regime then in June 2026 released FPL leader Mahmoud Sallah, who promptly launched a restructuring and recruitment drive. [63] Multiple Paris-based investigative outlets reported that the Haftar regime provided the FPL with vehicles and weapons as part of Sallah’s release and promised to provide additional equipment “in the coming months,” although the same sources have since reported that the LAAF has confined Sallah to southwestern Libya to keep him as a bargaining chip. [64] The Haftar regime has also strengthened ties with the FLA, infringing on Algeria’s traditional role as the primary interlocutor with Malian Tuareg rebels. The FGS had deployed over 2,000 soldiers and military vehicles to reclaim towns captured by opposition forces, but Al Shabaab's ambush near Leego halted their advance, with claims of up to 413 federal soldiers killed. The attack utilized vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and possibly drones, marking a tactical escalation for Al Shabaab. somalia.content: The First Domino: Uganda's Withdrawal and the Unravelling of Somalia's Security Architecture - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide The First Domino: Uganda’s Withdrawal and the Unravelling of Somalia’s Security Architecture October 29, 2026 5 min read KAMPALA , Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia, Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced, marking the first concrete step in a drawdown that comes just days after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud asked Kampala to delay the departure from strategic locations in southern Somalia. In a post on X, Muhoozi said: “As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers.” The statement did not specify the number of troops involved, the locations affected, or whether the withdrawal would be conducted in phases. The announcement follows reports that President Mohamud had appealed to President Yoweri Museveni to delay the withdrawal from Barawe, Bulo Marer, Qoryoley, and Janaale, to allow Somali forces more time to prepare to take over security responsibilities. Whether the withdrawal has been adjusted to accommodate that request is not clear. The Funding Crisis Behind the Withdrawal Uganda’s decision is rooted in a funding crisis that has been building for months, and it is a direct consequence of the structural weaknesses documented in FTL Somalia’s analysis of Somalia’s $1 billion security bill . That analysis, drawing on the World Bank’s 2026 Public Finance Review, warned that the planned AUSSOM drawdown could force the government to assume costs it cannot afford or preside over a decline in security capacity as external funding recedes. The crisis deepened when the United States informed the African Union that it would not support extending the UN logistical support arrangement for AUSSOM beyond the current mandate, which expires on December 31, 2026. The UN Support Office in Somalia provides food, fuel, water, medical support, and casualty evacuation for the mission’s roughly 11,200 soldiers and 680 police officers. Without that support, AUSSOM’s operations become logistically untenable. As FTL Somalia reported, the UN support office has already begun preparing for liquidation, issuing a public tender seeking auctioneers to sell generators, medical equipment, prefabricated accommodation, and heavy machinery valued at approximately $30 million. The drawdown is no longer a threat. It is happening. Uganda’s Dual Role Uganda’s presence in Somalia has two tracks. Under AUSSOM, Uganda contributes approximately 4,500 troops to the multilateral mission. Separately, Uganda maintains a bilateral force of roughly 2,000 personnel under a security agreement signed with Mogadishu in late 2024. Muhoozi’s statement did not clarify whether the withdrawal affects the AUSSOM contingent, the bilateral force, or both. Uganda’s Defence Minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, said in August 2026 that Uganda would remain in Somalia even if the AU mission ended, citing the bilateral agreement. Muhoozi’s announcement appears to contradict that position, or at least to suggest that a full withdrawal is now the preferred course. The Security Gap The withdrawal will place additional pressure on the Somali National Army to take over positions currently secured by Ugandan forces, including areas around Mogadishu and its approaches where Al-Shabaab has repeatedly carried out attacks. Ugandan troops have been instrumental in protecting critical government facilities, including Aden Adde International Airport and Mogadishu Port. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Entebbe meeting , President Mohamud’s request for Ugandan troops to stay longer was a tacit acknowledgment that Somali forces are not yet ready to assume full security responsibility. Muhoozi’s announcement suggests that Uganda is proceeding with the withdrawal regardless, or at least beginning a process that will be difficult to reverse. The structural weakness of the Somali security sector is not new. As documented in FTL Dhambaal’s 2021 report, “AMISOM: A Rescue Mission in Need of Rescue” , the mission originally scoped for 8,000 troops and six months grew into a 20,000-person operation spanning every federal member state. The report warned that troop-contributing countries had developed elaborate systems for deducting from soldiers’ allowances, and that the AU mission had expanded far beyond its agreed strategic locations. The current withdrawal is the latest chapter in a long history of external actors deciding when and how to leave, while the Somali state struggles to build the capacity to secure itself. Critical Note Muhoozi’s announcement is a social media post, not a formal military order, and it lacks the operational detail that a withdrawal of this significance requires. It does not say how many troops are leaving, from which bases, or whether the bilateral force will remain. It does not address President Mohamud’s request for a delay. And it does not explain how the handover will be managed without creating gaps that Al-Shabaab can exploit. The broader context is one of a mission unravelling under financial pressure. The United States has withdrawn its support for the logistics that sustain AUSSOM. The European Union has reduced its funding. The African Union owes months of arrears to troop-contributing countries. Uganda is the first major contributor to act on the warnings it has been issuing for months. Others may follow. For Somalia, the message is stark. The international scaffolding that has supported its security for two decades is being dismantled, and the withdrawal is beginning before the Somali National Army is ready to stand on its own. Muhoozi’s words, “handing over security to our Somali brothers,” frame the withdrawal as a transfer of responsibility. Whether it becomes a transfer or an abandonment will depend on what happens in the weeks and months ahead, and on whether the Somali government can fill the gap that Uganda is leaving behind. The Dhambaal’s warning from 2021, that the “African solutions to African problems” narrative is crippled, has never been more relevant. Sign In What's Included Exclusive Stories Daily ePaper Access Smart Market Tools Curated Investment Ideas Ad-lite Experience Subscription PTI Representational image Equipped with guns, the current generation of Somali pirates has taken to the high seas and has been hijacking commercial vessels by herding sailors into cramped quarters and holding hostages for several months before paying huge sums in ransom. This comes after several years of efforts by international navies to suppress acts of piracy along the coast of Somalia. The seizure of the Honour 25 clearly demonstrates the dangers that accompany such situations. The oil tanker was heading to Somalia when gunmen seized control of the ship and took the 17-member crew hostage on April 21, 2026. The crew was held hostage for several months as efforts were made for their release. However, while Somali security personnel attempted to liberate the vessel in September, five members of the crew lost their lives. This assault has once again raised the issue of the possible return of piracy in Somalia against the backdrop of the Iranian war affecting maritime activity and military focus on other waters. CNN's article focuses on the issue of how changing priorities in security, valuable cargo, and the possibility of making money through ransom might provide pirates with new opportunities for an attack. Live Events An ordinary voyage turned into a five-month hostage ordeal The Honour 25 was transporting about 2,700 tonnes of diesel oil from Oman to Mogadishu, the capital city of Somalia, when the attack by the pirates occurred. In accordance with CNN reports, Syed Hussain Yousuf, second engineer on board, received an alert regarding the possible pirate attack prior to the gunfire being opened. Within minutes, armed individuals got on board and ordered the crew members to assemble on the bridge. The Honour 25 had seventeen crew members on board. Most of the time, the sailors were confined to the bridge, which is described as a very small area where the crew members had to stay seated and move around only if led by the kidnappers for toilet use. Yasir Khan, the chief engineer aboard the ship, survived after being shot in the leg. In an interview with CNN, he mentioned that there was no warning system, no security guards, and no other safety precautions against piracy. He also noted that the ship's engines and generators were in poor shape. The pirates demanded a multi-million-dollar ransom for the release of the ship. The negotiations were ongoing when the crew was held hostage, but the crisis was resolved by a security operation conducted on September 29. According to the Somali authorities, five people among the crew were killed before the ship. There have been some conflicting reports about how they died. Why Somali pirates are returning to the high seas Piracy in Somalia had become a serious menace to international shipping in the last years of the decade between 2000 and 2010. There had been attacks where gangs hijacked cargo ships and took their crews hostage, and it led to the disruption of shipping through the western part of the Indian Ocean. The reduction in such attacks was not because the factors that fostered the act ceased to exist. CNN noted that economic instability in Somalia, together with new openings arising from the Iran war, has encouraged pirates to attack vessels again. The war has made the military concentrate on the Persian Gulf and the Bab el-Mandeb strait due to the Houthis' attacks on commercial vessels. According to CNN, there is less military presence around Somalia due to the shift of the US military's attention to the region. The conflict has also led to increased prices for oil. The tankers loaded with oil provide the possibility of collecting money as a ransom from pirates, which makes them attractive targets. Honour 25 is not the only ship involved in the wave. According to CNN, there have been cases when six ships were seized at once at some point during the summer, with about 90 crew members in captivity. Another organisation has voiced its worries over the results of the hijacking: the International Maritime Organization. According to information from October, 44 seafarers were released from three ships, including Honour 25, with five of them perishing during the rescue operations. How piracy threatens shipping costs far beyond Somalia Beyond those who are confronted at gunpoint, there is the risk to the shipping process, which may be disturbed and made more costly because ships will need to reroute to navigate the seas safely. According to CNN, rising insurance premiums have followed from increased security risks for ships in transit. In some cases, ships have needed to travel via Africa to avoid perilous waters and have incurred additional costs in fuel and time to do so. These costs may eventually make their way to consumers, since oil and other products rely on shipping systems and additional costs of transport and insurance could increase delivery fees. There may be vulnerabilities of smaller firms. In this case, CNN reported concerns regarding ships that do not have the same security measures as larger ships. As far as the Honour 25 ship is concerned, there was no security on board when the pirates boarded the ship. Piracy is, therefore, more than just a story about armed men boarding commercial vessels. Piracy is about the vulnerability of the vessel, the funds that can be raised through ransom and the abilities of international security forces to ensure that the major shipping routes remain safe. The recovery of the Honour 25 meant an end to a long period of imprisonment, but it took a very high price to pay. As the war in Iran affects the security of the seas and the economics of seafaring, the resurgence of piracy is another problem that needs to be addressed. football.summary: أسفرت قرعة دور المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا عن تشكيل مجموعة قوية للهلال السوداني، حيث انضم إلى المجموعة الرابعة التي تضم بيراميدز المصري وحوريا كوناكري الغيني والمغرب الفاسي. يعتبر الهلال السوداني من الأندية العريقة في أفريقيا، ويأمل في تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في هذه البطولة. في سياق متصل، حقق الهلال فوزاً على إيغل نوار بهدفين في مباراة سابقة ضمن البطولة، مما يعزز من معنويات الفريق قبل انطلاق دور المجموعات. كما شهدت الساحة الرياضية السودانية بعض الأحداث المثيرة، حيث انتقد صحفي سوداني إدارة نادي المريخ بعد خروج الفريق من المنافسات، بينما أكد موقع مصري تأهل المريخ للمجموعات. يتطلع عشاق كرة القدم في السودان إلى أداء مميز من الهلال في هذه النسخة من البطولة.
